Q1: Dispatch Call A (Maple St, 7.8) — the chest pain call is the highest-scored waiting call, so the medic unit goes there. No call reaches 9.0, but the threshold is an escalation trigger, not a dispatch gate — holding a medic idle while a 7.8 cardiac call waits costs lives.
Q2: Dispatch Call A (Pine Rd, 8.4) — the kitchen fire scores highest, so the engine goes there. Neither call hits 9.0, which only means no mutual-aid escalation is triggered; the highest urgency still wins the next unit.
Q3: Dispatch Call A (1st St, 8.9) — a reported person trapped with smoke showing edges out the elevator rescue, so the ladder truck goes there. Both sit just under 9.0, which means no extra escalation, but never a reason to hold the truck idle.
Q4: Dispatch Call A (Hill Rd, 7.1) — the conscious diabetic emergency outscores the event standby, so the BLS unit goes to the diabetic emergency. A standby detail is a routine low-urgency assignment that must never outrank a scored medical call.
Q5: Dispatch Call A (River St, 8.1) — difficulty breathing scores highest by a hair and breathing emergencies deteriorate fast, so the medic goes there. Near-ties are resolved by the score, not by guessing; 8.1 beats 8.0, full stop.
Q6: Dispatch Call A (Main St, 6.8) — the vehicle fire is the highest-scored call, so the engine goes there. Below 9.0 no mutual-aid escalation is required, but the offered aid can be accepted to cover the brush fire near homes so no exposure is left unaddressed.
Q7: Dispatch Call A (Park Ave, 7.5) — a multi-vehicle accident with injuries needing command oversight is the only waiting call, so the battalion chief goes there. A single waiting call is still a queue; idle command units with a live incident is a failure, not prudence.
Q8: Dispatch Call A (Cedar Ln, 8.7) — stroke symptoms inside a closing treatment window are the highest-scored call, so the medic goes there. Time-criticality is exactly why it scores highest; holding the unit while a stroke patient waits squanders the treatment window.
Q9: Dispatch Call A (Summit Dr, 5.9) — the gas leak is the only scored waiting call, so the engine goes there. A modest score means a routine dispatch, not a hold; an empty queue with an idle engine while an evacuated gas leak waits is the failure the principle is designed to prevent.
